replies.author: @Thegoodthebadandthefleshtuber
replies.text:
Scanlines (ferry owners) have announced they will not be stopping operation, hence it will still be possible to use the ferry and it's expected to be at half price of the tunnel. The financial predictions for the tunnel includes stopping the ferries, both at Rødby-Puttgarten (so next to the tunnel) and Gedser-Rostock. However both lines are gearing up for competing directly with new ferries and stuff. The ferry takes 45 minutes of actual sailing time (so not including showing up in advance). It's generally seen as a good break for drivers and there is duty free shops on board, so it's expected that the ferries will survive.

It has been a hot political topic that the expected income from the tunnel to repay it is too optimistic even before considering the competition from the ferries. As a standalone investment, the tunnel makes no sense. It has to consider the boost to the economy in general for it to make sense. They are moving profits from the Great Belt Bridge to the tunnel to make it more feasible and hence the tunnel has broken the promise of the bridge getting cheaper to use once repaid. A number of people aren't particularly happy about that.

replies.author: @jesperfuglsang
replies.text:
@gerardflynn3899 Scandinavia is a historical, cultural, and linguistic region rather than just a strictly geographical one. Since the mid-19th century, the term has specifically referred to the three kingdoms of Denmark, Norway, and Sweden, which share mutually intelligible North Germanic languages and deeply intertwined histories (such as the Kalmar Union).
While Denmark isn't located on the Scandinavian Peninsula (which is a purely geographical term for the landmass shared by Norway, Sweden, and northern Finland), it is still one of the three core countries that make up Scandinavia itself. In fact, the word "Scandinavia" originally referred to Scania (Skåne)—the southernmost tip of modern-day Sweden, which was historically part of Denmark for centuries!

The same will apply for all of Sweden.

replies.author: @ahkkariq7406
replies.text:
@annabackman3028 
The term "Scandinavia" exists in various forms, the geographical definition being one of them. 
I am fully aware that there are only three Scandinavian countries, and that they share close linguistic, historical, and cultural ties. This does not preclude the existence of another interpretation of "Scandinavia"—in this case, referring to a part of Finland that offers a direct route through Sweden toward the south, should one wish to drive to the western part of the European continent. Consequently, parts of Finland are included in this context. 
This is not to say that I do not respect the Finns' desire to define themselves as being outside of Scandinavia; however, I am from Northern Norway myself, and I have frequently driven through both Finland and Sweden to reach the southern parts of Norway. The same applies to those parts of Finland that I have passed through on all those occasions.
